subject: brutalistBlock
pitch:
Category: Architecture.
Subject: brutalist housing block.
Style: raw concrete brutalism.
reasoning:
I'm planning a brutalist housing block as a static model—thinking of it as a long concrete slab on pilotis with deep loggia balconies, brise-soleil screens, and a separate lift/stair tower, since static models don't require joints.

I'm settling on real-world proportions around 72m long, 20m deep, 12 storeys over 6m pilotis, with board-formed concrete texture, Corbusier-style colored accents on balcony walls, and a handful of glowing windows for atmosphere. Part count should land in the 180-340 range, well within the 1000-part budget.

For the hundreds of repeated loggia elements, I'm considering merging geometries grouped by color, but I need to watch out for UV conflicts — merging boxes with overlapping 0-1 UVs could break the paint baking since each part's chart likely relies on its own UV layout. Safer approach: keep large painted surfaces like the slab and piers as fewer, bigger parts rather than merging many small painted boxes together.

For repeated small details, flat colors merge cleanly since they're handled through atlas cells with no UV dependency, and textured planes like windows merge fine too since they each reuse the full texture via standard UVs. I'll settle on flat concrete colors (keeping the palette under the 64-color limit) for things like balcony slab edges so they can be merged safely, while reserving actual paint for larger, separate parts.

The real design question is how to build the façade structure itself: floor slabs per level (roughly a dozen long boxes) painted with board-formed concrete, plus vertical party-wall fins between loggias. The tricky part is whether merging many painted fins into one geometry per face is safe, since I suspect the baker unwraps charts per-triangle rather than using true UVs (the separate "SURFACE" attribute suggests this), so merged painted geometry might get unpredictable chart packing.

Working through the math, texel density on a texture like 1024 or 2048 px spread over a building-sized painted area comes out coarse — something like 6-12 cm per texel — which is marginal for showing board-formed concrete striations or 30 cm formwork lines, though panel joints at roughly 1.2 m scale should still read fine, so I'll lean on larger-scale features for the paint and consider whether a smaller building or supplemental textures could help with finer detail.

I'm trying to cut down total painted area by being selective — only painting the visible concrete surfaces that matter (pilotis, slab fascias, end walls, roof structures, lift tower) and using flat colors for hidden or small elements, which brings the estimate down to around 5000 m² and gives a workable ~24 texels/meter on a 2048 sheet. I'm also considering shrinking the building itself to roughly 11 storeys, 66 m long and 18 m deep, and starting to define the floor height, pilotis height, and overall block dimensions as concrete parameters.

Now I'm thinking through the lift tower placement — a separate volume connected by bridges every few floors, brutalist-style like Trellick Tower's service tower. I'm weighing whether to put it at the back near one end versus trying to keep things roughly centered on x=0, since an asymmetrical tower placement would shift the bounding box center away from where I want it.

I'll go with two service towers at the back, placed symmetrically at x=±17, each rising above the main slab's roofline and connected by bridges at floor 3, 6, and 9 plus ground level. For the front facade, I'm working out the loggia rhythm: 3.3 m bay widths giving twenty bays across the 66 m width, with vertical dividers marking each bay boundary.

Now I'm defining the depth of the facade — the main wall plane sits further back while the loggia frame projects forward about 2.4-3 m, with floor slabs spanning the full depth at each level and dividers framing the loggia openings.

For the back facade, I'll keep it simpler with ribbon windows and recessed corridor decks with railings every third floor, plus some bays getting horizontal brise-soleil louvers for variation. For the loggia backs, I'm thinking of a seeded random color pick among a small palette (red, ochre, blue, green, white) to add visual rhythm across the facade.

I'm planning 220 colored panels across 11×20 bays, merged by color into efficient groups, with window glazing textures (frame, mullions, sky reflection, curtain hints) applied per bay and merged by texture variant—aiming for 5-12 distinct textures covering windows, entrance glass, railings, and signage.

For end-wall treatments, I'm considering a bold building sign ("UNITÉ" with numerals) and a large geometric mural evoking Modulor-style figures. Lit windows get a separate warm-glow texture with glow strength 0.8, keeping unlit windows dark by default, and for loggias I'm skipping railings in favor of a simple 0.9m concrete parapet fascia at the front edge.

I'm refining the loggia parapet as colored concrete panels sized per bay, deciding between solid panels versus metal-bar railings, and settling on painted/concrete panel variations that partially conceal the window below. For the back wall, I'm layering a colored panel behind a slightly offset window plane with a dark frame and glass texture, so the coloring shows through around the window's edges.

Now I'm defining a seeded color palette (red, yellow, blue, green, white, grey concrete) weighted for variety, then tallying part counts by merging similar elements: wall panels, parapets, and window textures grouped by color, with other pieces kept separate. For the floor slabs spanning the full building length with overhangs, I'm creating individual painted concrete parts, designing a custom concrete texture with horizontal board marks, offset vertical plank joints, and a grid of dark tie holes to mimic real formwork.

I'm reconsidering the tie hole size and spacing against the texture resolution, deciding to simplify by skipping tiny tie holes and instead focusing on larger pour lines, vertical rain stain streaks, mossy discoloration near the base, and soot staining using stretched noise patterns.

Writing concrete paint function...

Adding board-line variation and rain streak staining...

For pilotis, I'm thinking of massive tapered piers spaced at regular intervals under the slab, maybe 11 positions evenly distributed across the x-axis.

I want Corbusier-style piers that widen toward the top rather than the bottom, using a vertical frustum shape going from a narrower box at the base to a wider one near the top.

For the ground level, I'm thinking of a glazed entrance lobby box between the central piers with a canopy, but skipping a full ground plinth since the brief doesn't call for one—just a few entrance steps as part of the building itself.

For the roof, I'm planning a composition of elements like Corbusier's rooftop terraces: a rooftop pavilion with a ramp, three lathed ventilation chimneys with flared tops, a water tank, stair-core and lift overrun towers, and a sculptural canopy.

For the towers themselves, I'm sketching a 7×6.5 plan rising to height 44, with narrow vertical slit windows and a top crown featuring a cantilevered box and small vent, connected to the main slab by covered walkway bridges positioned between the back wall and tower faces.

Now I'm working out bridge placement across storeys 2, 5, and 8 for each tower, with floor slabs, roof boxes, and windowed side walls, plus ground-level entrances, while also planning the back façade's ribbon windows and balconies bay by bay.

For the core, I'll model it as one large concrete box spanning the full height and width, with floor slabs projecting slightly beyond it and the end walls capping off at x=±33, keeping decks at every third storey with simple parapet railings.

The end walls become the main canvas—adding end cap boxes to cover the loggia depth above the core, then placing a mural, number plaque, and slit window column on each end face.

The mural is a painted plane facing outward at each end wall, textured with an abstract Corbusier-style SVG: color block grids, a Modulor figure outline, and a spiral sun motif. I'm also considering large painted numerals on the end wall to act as block signage, like a bold "7" on one end.

For the roof, I'm layering in parapet detail, ventilation stacks, a rooftop pavilion with a ramp and vaulted form, planter boxes, a pergola, a water tank on steel legs with antennas, and glowing skylight cones under a sculptural canopy. At ground level I'm adding an entrance lobby with canopy and a stair placed between the piers.

For the facade texture, I'm thinking about colored infill walls between the piers with glazed lobby bays and a utility wall, then sprinkling in loggia details like potted plants, hanging laundry, umbrellas, and satellite dishes to give each unit its own personality.

Now I'm budgeting the triangle count against the 60k limit, weighing merged versus separate geometry for the loggia dividers. I'm leaning toward flat grey concrete with subtle tonal variation for the dividers rather than full paint textures, since it's cheaper while still reading correctly under the lighting.

Let me simplify by making each divider one continuous tall box spanning full height instead of per-storey segments, cutting part count to 21 dividers plus 12 crossing slabs — though the painted surface area comes out larger than I'd like.

Tallying total painted area: core box faces, divider surfaces, slab fascias and top/bottom faces, the numbers balloon to roughly 30,000 m² if every hidden surface counts. That would crush the texel density down to around 9.9 px/unit, which is too low — I need to reconsider whether hidden surfaces actually get painted.

Working out the texel density gives about 14.5 texels per meter at 2048 resolution, roughly 7cm per texel, which seems fine. I'm reconsidering whether to simplify the slab strips to flat concrete color rather than fully painted, since the fascia is the most visible horizontal surface.

I'll keep paint sheet at 2048 wide within a 4096 atlas budget, limit colors to around 30 flat tones, and start defining layout constants for building dimensions.

Now I'm working out the depth asymmetry—pilotis height, floor thickness, number of stories, and where the core walls sit front and back—so the massing reads correctly with the back deliberately offset deeper than the front.

Each storey's clear interior space runs from the slab top to the next slab bottom, giving a clear height of 2.6 after subtracting slab thickness. For the loggia I'm working out the parapet at 1.0 above the floor and placing the back wall window with a sill around 0.35 up from the floor.

Now I'm figuring out the bay spacing: dividing the 66m length into 20 bays of 3.3m each, with dividers at each bay boundary, thicker end caps, and slabs extending slightly past the core footprint to cover them.

I'm also checking for z-fighting where the slab's front fascia edge meets the divider's front face at the same depth coordinate—they're coplanar, which could cause rendering overlap issues, so I need to offset one of them slightly.

I should align core and divider end faces at x=±33.7 so they only meet at edges rather than overlapping, avoiding z-fighting; but I need to check whether the divider's back face at z=6.6 coincides with the core's front face over the same x-range, since two coplanar overlapping faces facing opposite directions would still cause flicker there.

I should keep slabs visible including the loggia floors and ceilings, and make sure dividers rest properly on slab 0 without hiding the pilotis below. Now I'm working out the pilotis layout — positioning columns along x at regular intervals with front and rear rows to support the slabs.

For the actual pier geometry I'm leaning toward using tapered box shapes, with the width running along x and the depth/height along z, trying to approximate a frustum-like tapered column shape rather than a simple cylinder.

I want each pier to feel Corbusier-like, so I'm considering a two-stage taper — thinner lower section widening into a chunkier upper section — possibly with a capital-like cap box at the top for added mass. But doubling parts per pier would push the count up significantly, so I'm weighing whether to simplify to one tapered part per pier instead of adding a separate capital piece.

Part counts aren't tight (under 1000, aiming near 300), so I'm roughing out totals: piers, slabs, and a front strip should keep things comfortably under 340. I'm laying out front and rear pier rows at regular x-intervals, with one row pulled slightly forward in z, Unité-style, and leaving the center pier open at x=0 to carve out a glazed entrance lobby with doors between the flanking piers.

Now I'm designing the lobby itself: a grey floor box, two glass shopfront planes with a door spanning the gap between the kept piers, protected by the overhanging slab above, plus a few step boxes leading up to it. I'm deciding to drop the center front pier entirely to open the span for glazing, keeping the outer piers standing behind the glass, and I'm planning a signboard above the entrance.

Since slab 0 is too thin to carry a sign, I'm adding a separate heavy fascia beam below its front edge, deep enough to hold a "RESIDENCE" text plane across most of the front width.

I'll name the building "MARLOWE HOUSE" and letter it in white on the dark beam, sizing it to fit within the beam height, with piers clearing underneath. I'm also darkening the underside paint of slab 0 for an ambient-occlusion effect, then defining the roof level as the top of the final storey slab, with parapet walls around the perimeter and tower elements positioned symmetrically along the facade.

For the towers, I'm placing them behind the bridge connection off the core's back face, extending them up past the roofline for a lift overrun, and detailing each as a painted concrete box with vertical slit windows on the side and back faces plus bridge doors facing the slab. I'm adding a crowning overhang box with a lift machine room and mast, plus horizontal banding ribs at the bridging floor levels and vertical corner buttresses for texture.

Now I'm working out the bridges connecting towers to the core at each bridging level, building them as closed concrete box tubes with window strips on both side faces, and writing a helper function to construct and orient window planes correctly on the +X and -X facing sides.

Since no joints get created, the SDK just treats this as a static model, so I'll skip calling any joint methods entirely. I'm keeping the merged parts colored white since the textures themselves carry the actual coloring, and I need to double-check the plane orientations show only front faces correctly. I'm deciding to skip extras like lampposts, trees, and fire-stair bridges, keeping focus purely on the building. Setting up differentiated surface treatment by face orientation: horizontal faces get a mossy tint via noise blending, bottom faces darken, and areas near the ground mix toward a muddy brown based on height.
